title: ASASSN-14ko flares in 2023-2025 occur up to 21 days later than the Payne et al. 2022 ephemeris predicts, and the period decrease became slower after 2021
abstract: ASASSN-14ko is a nuclear transient in ESO 253-G003 with flares that repeat approximately every 115 d. Payne et al. (2022) published a timing model with a period derivative Pdot = -0.0026, fit to flares up to 2021 November. We tested this model with data that it did not use: ASAS-SN Sky Patrol v2 g-band photometry to 2025 February, our own aperture photometry of 382 Swift/UVOT visits (2020-2026), and TESS full-frame-image photometry, which includes sector 98 (2025 October-November). We measured flare times with several markers (UV peak, optical half-rise, template shift, polynomial peak). We calibrated the offset of each marker on 2018-2021 flares. After 2022 the flares occur later than the published prediction: by +3 to +6 d in 2022-2023, by +6 to +17 d in 2023-2024, and by +21 d in 2025 November (TESS). Three instruments agree. From the Swift-UV-peak and optical-rise markers, the local period decreased by 0.41 +/- 0.09 d per cycle in 2018-2021 but by only 0.12 +/- 0.06 d per cycle in 2021-2025 (z = 2.7, approximate). The mean local period in 2023-2025 is 107.45 +/- 0.32 d. The Payne et al. 2022 model predicts 105.3 d. The strength of the evidence for a change of Pdot depends on the data set. A re-fit of the published 2014-2021 peak times with a free jitter (Pdot = -0.00214) still agrees with the 2022-2025 times (p = 0.26), because its forecast spread is +/- 3-8 d. A re-fit with the Payne et al. error treatment (Pdot = -0.00234) is rejected by the optical-rise times (p = 0.003). Joint fits prefer a change of Pdot near 2021 by Delta BIC = 4.8 to 32. Limitations: we had no ground-based optical data after 2025 February; flare shapes changed in 2022-2023, so the flare markers can shift; our UVOT photometry does not use the HEASoft pipeline. We give forecasts for the 2026-2027 flares (for example, a peak near 2026-11-18 if the 2023-2025 period stays constant, against 2026-10-18 from the Payne et al. 2022 model). These forecasts can be tested directly.

display.caption: Observed minus predicted flare times relative to the Payne et al. 2022 ephemeris (P0 = 115.2 d, Pdot = -0.0026). Grey squares: published peak times used in that fit. Blue: Swift UVW2 peaks. Orange: optical half-rise times (ASAS-SN g). Green: ASAS-SN template times (biased for the broad 2022 flares). Red stars: TESS half-rise times (2018, 2025). Each marker series is shifted by its constant offset, calibrated on 2018-2021 flares. Purple: a re-fit of the published times with free jitter. The shaded area is out of sample.

Local period from consecutive well-timed flares (Swift UV peaks, optical half-rise times). Yellow lines: separate linear fits for 2018-2021 (-0.41 +/- 0.09 d per cycle) and 2021-2025 (-0.12 +/- 0.06 d per cycle). Dashed: Payne et al. 2022 model. Purple: free-jitter re-fit of published peaks. Error bars include a 1 d timing jitter per flare. Consecutive periods share one flare time.

Light curves aligned on the Payne et al. 2022 predicted peak times. (a) TESS nucleus photometry of the 2018 (cycle 14) and 2025 (cycle 38) flares: the rise shapes are the same, but the 2025 rise is 17 d later. (b) Swift UVW2 for cycles 21, 30 and 33: the source stayed quiescent at the predicted cycle-33 peak and peaked 14 d later. (c) ASAS-SN g stacks of 2020-2021 and 2023-2024 flares.
